prompt: The five fields of `Loose` (three `bool`s, an `int32` and an `int64`) add up to 15 bytes, yet `unsafe.Sizeof` says 32 on amd64. Where do the other 17 come from?
hint: Look at the offsets the program printed, and at where each field could have started.

choices.text: A `bool` takes a whole 8-byte word on a 64-bit machine, like an `int64`
choices.why: `Tight` puts its three `bool`s at offsets 12, 13 and 14, one byte each. The gaps in `Loose` come from what follows each `bool`.

choices.text: The runtime adds a hidden header to every struct for the garbage collector
choices.why: `tally.Entry` is 72 bytes and its fields add up to exactly 72, so there is no header. The extra bytes in `Loose` sit between and after its fields.

choices.text: Padding, so that each field starts at a multiple of its alignment
choices.why: Right. Seven bytes after `Cached` put `Bytes` at 8, three after `TLS` put `Status` at 20, and seven after `Retry` round 25 up to 32.

choices.text: `unsafe.Sizeof` counts the memory the fields point to
choices.why: None of `Loose`'s fields is a pointer. And the documentation says `Sizeof` does not include memory a value refers to: for a slice it is the 24-byte header only.

prompt: On linux/amd64, what does `unsafe.Sizeof` return for `struct { A bool; B int64; C bool }`?
hint: Place each field at a multiple of its alignment, then round the end up to the largest alignment.

prompt: `fieldalignment` reports `Summary has 24 leading bytes of pointer data but optimal value is 16` for lesson 1's `tally.Summary`. What is the right response in `hits`?
hint: How many `Summary` values does one run of `hits` make?

choices.text: Leave it: one `Summary` per run saves nothing
choices.why: Right. The diagnostic is about how far the collector scans for pointers. Saved once per run it is nothing, and the analyzer's documentation says these findings very rarely matter.

choices.text: Reorder it at once, because the struct wastes 8 bytes of padding
choices.why: The report is not about size: `Summary` has no padding. It is about pointer bytes, the part of the value the collector scans.

choices.text: Add `go vet` to CI, which runs the same check on every build
choices.why: `fieldalignment` is deliberately not part of `go vet`; its documentation says so, because its findings so rarely matter.

choices.text: Make both maps pointers to maps so they scan faster
choices.why: A map value is already a pointer to the runtime's table. Wrapping it in another pointer adds an indirection and changes nothing the analyzer measured.

prompt: A team runs `fieldalignment` over a service and proposes to apply every suggested order. Which of these are sound objections? Choose all that apply.
hint: One objection comes from the analyzer's documentation, one from the arithmetic of how many values exist.

choices.text: Fields updated by separate goroutines may share a cache line
choices.why: Right. The documentation names this false sharing: the compact order can make two goroutines slow each other down, and there the padding was doing a job.

choices.text: A struct that exists a few times saves nothing worth a diff
choices.why: Right. The million-element slice halved from 32 to 16 MB; one value saves 16 bytes, and the readable order is worth more.

choices.text: Code that uses `unsafe.Offsetof` on those fields will stop compiling
choices.why: `Offsetof` is worked out by the compiler for the struct as it is declared now, so moving a field changes the constant and nothing breaks. A hand-written offset would break, silently.

choices.text: The collector cannot scan a struct whose pointer fields come first
choices.why: It is the reverse: putting pointers first lets the collector stop scanning sooner. That is what the pointer-bytes diagnostic is about.

prompt: How does the garbage collector treat an `unsafe.Pointer` and a `uintptr` holding the same address?
hint: One of the two is a pointer type and the other is an integer type.

choices.text: Both keep the object alive, since they hold the same address
choices.why: The address is the same, the type is not. The `alive` program held the entry's address in a `uintptr` and the cleanup ran anyway.

choices.text: Neither: values from package `unsafe` are invisible to the collector
choices.why: An `unsafe.Pointer` is still a pointer to the runtime; only the type checks are switched off. That is why pattern 3 must convert back within one expression.

choices.text: The collector updates the `uintptr` when it moves the object
choices.why: The documentation says the opposite: it will not update a `uintptr`'s value if the object moves, nor will the integer keep the object from being reclaimed.

choices.text: It follows the first as a reference and ignores the second
choices.why: Right. The collector finds live objects by following pointers, and a `uintptr` is not one, so an object reachable only through one is garbage.

prompt: The `field` program reads `Status` three ways and all three print `404`, yet `go vet` flags the third, where the address is first stored in `u := uintptr(...)`. Why is code that printed the right answer wrong?
hint: Think about what can happen between two statements that cannot happen inside one expression.

choices.text: `go vet` rejects any arithmetic on addresses, valid or not
choices.why: The first version does the same arithmetic in one expression, which is pattern 3, and `vet` said nothing about it.

choices.text: Between the two lines the object exists only as an integer, which the collector and stack copying ignore
choices.why: Right. On this run nothing moved and nothing was collected in that moment. On another, a growing stack or a collection between the lines leaves `u` naming memory that is no longer the entry.

choices.text: A stored `uintptr` loses its upper 32 bits
choices.why: A `uintptr` is wide enough to hold any address on its platform; that is its definition. Nothing is truncated.

choices.text: `Offsetof` gives the wrong answer outside a single expression
choices.why: `Offsetof` is a constant the compiler computes; it is 56 wherever it is written. The problem is the address, not the offset.

prompt: Which of these lines is valid under the documented patterns for `unsafe.Pointer`? Assume `p` points into an allocated struct `s` and `b` is a non-empty `[]byte`.
hint: Pattern 3 has three conditions: one expression, still inside the original allocation, and never nil.

choices.text: `end := unsafe.Add(unsafe.Pointer(&b[0]), len(b))`
choices.why: That points one byte past the end of the slice's allocation. C allows it; the documentation lists exactly this as invalid, and `unsafe.Add` keeps the same rules.

choices.text: `f := unsafe.Pointer(uintptr(p) + unsafe.Offsetof(s.f))`
choices.why: Right. Pointer to `uintptr`, arithmetic and back, all in one expression, landing on a field inside the same struct.

choices.text: `u := uintptr(p); q := unsafe.Pointer(u + 8)`
choices.why: The address is stored in a variable between the two conversions, which is the invalid form `go vet` reported in the `field` program.

choices.text: `q := unsafe.Pointer(uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(nil)) + unsafe.Offsetof(s.f))`
choices.why: The documentation says the pointer must point into an allocated object, so it may not be nil, and gives this very line as invalid.

prompt: Building the `cast` program with `-race` stopped it on the cut record, because `-race` also turns on the compiler's ___ instrumentation of `unsafe.Pointer` conversions.
hint: The same check `-gcflags=all=-d=...` turns on by name.

prompt: On a run without checkptr, `cast` printed `18 bytes: quick   3602879701896396948` for the record cut one byte into the status, and `go vet` reported nothing. Why did `vet` stay silent?
hint: Ask what `vet` can know about the length of `rec`.

choices.text: The `unsafeptr` check is only enabled by `go vet -all`
choices.why: `unsafeptr` is in `go vet`'s default set; it is what flagged the `field` program. It looks for a different mistake.

choices.text: The read happened inside `encoding/binary`, which `vet` skips
choices.why: The cast is in `quick`, in the program itself. `encoding/binary` is the half that panicked with a bounds error.

choices.text: Reading memory is allowed; only writing through a cast is invalid
choices.why: The rules are about which conversions are valid, whatever is done with the pointer afterwards. Reading past an allocation is as invalid as writing there.

choices.text: It depends on `len(rec)` at run time, which code cannot show
choices.why: Right. `vet` reads the code, and the code is the same for the 25-byte record that works and the 18-byte one that does not.

prompt: Why does an ordinary `string(b)` conversion copy the bytes of `b`?
hint: Compare what each of the two types promises about its contents.

choices.text: A string's bytes never change and a slice's do, so the string needs its own
choices.why: Right. Without the copy, a later write to `b` would change a value the language promises is immutable, which is what `mutate` showed.

choices.text: Strings are stored in UTF-16 internally, so every byte has to be converted
choices.why: Go strings are bytes, usually UTF-8, and the conversion changes nothing in them. The copy is about ownership, not encoding.

choices.text: The garbage collector cannot follow a pointer into a slice
choices.why: It can, and does: a slice's header holds an ordinary pointer to its array. `zc.String` shares those bytes and the collector keeps them alive.

choices.text: A string needs a terminating zero byte that a slice lacks
choices.why: That is C. A Go string carries its length in its header and has no terminator; `unsafe.String(p, n)` takes the length as an argument.

prompt: In the benchmarks, `k := string(path)` followed by `hits[k]` allocated nothing for a 10-byte key and 48 bytes for a 41-byte one. Up to how many bytes can a converted string that does not escape be built in a buffer on the stack?
hint: The constant is `tmpStringBufSize` in `runtime/string.go`.

prompt: `hits[string(path)]` allocated nothing, but `hits[string(path)]++` allocated 16 bytes on every call, with the key already in the map. Why the difference?
hint: One of the two expressions may have to store something.

choices.text: Increments are slower, so the runtime caches each key's string in a side table
choices.why: There is no cache; the 16 bytes are the size class for the 10-byte key, built as a string on every call.

choices.text: The benchmark loop allocates the string, not the map expression
choices.why: The lookup benchmarks use the same `b.Loop()` and report 0 B/op, so the loop allocates nothing.

choices.text: `++` inserts the key when it is missing, and a stored key must be an immutable string
choices.why: Right. A lookup only compares bytes, so the compiler passes them without building a string. An insert keeps the key, and a key has to be a real, immutable string.

choices.text: Map values of type `int` are boxed on every write
choices.why: Map values are stored in place in the map's table; an `int` is not boxed. The allocation is the key.

prompt: `paths` counted 20,000 requests under about 1,536 keys with `zc.String(fields[2])`, against 8 keys with `string(fields[2])`. What happened to the keys?
hint: Read what `bufio.Scanner.Bytes` says about the array its result points into.

choices.text: The map's hash seed is random, so the zero-copy keys were hashed differently
choices.why: The seed changes where keys sit in the table, never what they read. Over a thousand keys contained a space or a newline, which no path does.

choices.text: A goroutine inside the scanner raced with the counting loop
choices.why: A `Scanner` runs on the caller's goroutine, and the race detector passed. One goroutine overwrote its own buffer.

choices.text: The collector freed the field slices and reused their memory
choices.why: A string from `unsafe.String` is a real pointer that keeps the bytes alive. Nothing was freed; the owner of the bytes rewrote them.

choices.text: They were windows onto the scanner's buffer, which later lines overwrote
choices.why: Right. Each key shared bytes with `sc.Bytes()`, and the scanner reused that buffer for the next lines, so stored keys changed into pieces of other lines.

prompt: `go doc unsafe` says packages that import it are not protected by the Go 1 compatibility guidelines. What does that mean for such a package?
hint: What does the promise give every other package?

choices.text: It is refused by `go vet` until it is marked with a build tag
choices.why: `vet` checks some conversions but refuses no package for importing `unsafe`; 101 packages of the standard library import it.

choices.text: It cannot be published to the module proxy
choices.why: The proxy serves any module; the compatibility promise is about Go releases, not about distribution.

choices.text: Nothing stops a later release from breaking it, without notice
choices.why: Right. The promise that a program keeps building and behaving the same way does not cover code relying on how the runtime lays out memory.

choices.text: It has to be rebuilt with `CGO_ENABLED=1`
choices.why: `unsafe` is part of the language and needs no C compiler; every program in this lesson built with the defaults.

prompt: Built with `GOARCH=386`, the `layout` program puts `tally.Entry`'s `Status` at offset 36, against 56 on amd64. What should code that reads that field through a pointer take from this?
hint: One way of writing the offset is right on both machines.

choices.text: Always write `unsafe.Offsetof(e.Status)`, never a number
choices.why: Right. `Offsetof` is a constant the compiler works out for the platform it is building, so it is 36 on 386 and 56 on amd64 with no change to the code.

choices.text: Hard-code 36 behind a `//go:build 386` tag and 56 elsewhere
choices.why: That works until a field is added or a third architecture is built, and then reads the wrong bytes in silence. The compiler already knows the answer for every platform.

choices.text: Avoid 32-bit targets, since Go no longer supports them
choices.why: Go 1.27.1 built and ran the 386 program on this machine in the same section. The offsets differ; the platform is supported.

choices.text: Reorder `tally.Entry` so `Status` comes first
choices.why: Offset 0 would match on both, but by accident, and only for that one field. The rule has to hold for every field read this way.

prompt: Match each bug from the lesson with what found it.
hint: One of them found nothing at all, and one tool is listed that found none of them.

pairs.left: a `uintptr` stored in a variable, then turned back into a pointer
eight bytes read where a record had one
a zero-copy string as a map key over the scanner's buffer
pairs.right: no tool: only a reader of the code
the operating system, with a segmentation fault

right_distractors: the tests `go test` runs by default

prompt: Put the steps of the lesson's rule for using `unsafe` in your own code in order.
hint: Nothing is written until something has been measured.
items: Measure the copy or allocation with a profile or a benchmark
Look for a safe version, such as `m[string(b)]` or `encoding/binary`
Isolate the unsafe code in one small package with its promise in the doc comments
Run `go test -race` and `go vet ./...` on it in CI, and again on every Go upgrade

prompt: `strings.Builder.String` returns `unsafe.String(unsafe.SliceData(b.buf), len(b.buf))`, the same zero-copy conversion as `zc.String`. Why is it safe there when `zc.String` broke `paths`?
hint: Ask who can write to the bytes after the string exists.

choices.text: Code in the standard library is exempt from the `unsafe.Pointer` rules
choices.why: The rules apply to every package that imports `unsafe`, the standard library included. `Builder` keeps them; what makes it safe is who can reach the buffer.

choices.text: The builder owns its buffer, never exposes it, and only appends past the end
choices.why: Right. No caller can reach `b.buf`, and appending writes beyond the length any returned string covers, so the promise is kept by the type rather than by every caller.

choices.text: `String` copies the buffer whenever the builder is used again
choices.why: There is no copy-on-write in `Builder`; `go doc -src` shows `String` is that one line. Growing the buffer allocates a new array, which leaves old strings alone.

choices.text: The race detector checks every `Builder` in tests
choices.why: `-race` finds two goroutines touching memory unsynchronised; it would not have caught `paths` either, which had one goroutine.

prompt: A colleague wants to speed up a function that looks lines up in a `map[string]Route`, keyed by the request path, by converting each `[]byte` path with `zc.String` before the lookup. Which statements are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of the benchmarks in the lesson are about exactly this, and one of the tools was run against exactly this bug.

choices.text: Writing `routes[string(path)]` already does the lookup without building a string
choices.why: Right. `BenchmarkLookup` and `BenchmarkLookupLong` showed 0 B/op for a 10-byte and a 41-byte key: the compiler handles a conversion inside an index expression.

choices.text: If the zero-copy string were ever stored, `-race` would not catch the damage
choices.why: Right. `paths` passed `vet`, `-race` and checkptr while its keys turned into pieces of other lines. One goroutine overwriting its own buffer is invisible to all three.

choices.text: checkptr would stop the program at the first `zc.String` call
choices.why: The conversion itself is valid: the pointer and length describe bytes inside one allocation. checkptr has nothing to object to at that moment.

choices.text: A map copies a key's bytes when it stores it, so storing is safe too
choices.why: A map stores the string header it was given, pointer and length. That is how `paths` filed counts under keys that later changed.

prompt: `go test` runs only a high-confidence subset of `vet` before a test binary, so the check that reports a `uintptr` turned back into a pointer, ___, needs `go vet ./...` as a CI step of its own.
hint: It printed `possible misuse of unsafe.Pointer` for the `field` program.
